Hon. ROBERT WEIR (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading of Bill No. 22, respecting the inspection and grading of hay and straw.

Before the second reading passes, I should like to say a few words, Mr. Speaker. It will be noticed that this bill makes a distinct change

Grading oj Hay and Straw
in policy. In the previous bill the regulations regarding hay and straw were in the bill itself. It is now proposed to put into the hands of the minister power to make regulations. I see no occasion for that. It is just another case of which we have seen so many examples in the last ten years, of taking power away from parliament and putting it into the hands of a department, no matter how able its officials may be. I have very great respect indeed for the officials of the Department of Agriculture, but I have noticed over a period of years one peculiarity in their point of view, and that is that they adopt the policy of making the penalties very extreme for any infraction of the rules and regulations which they make. They appear to go ,on the principle of the Turkish sultan who made it his boast that, when he found a baker selling bread of short weight, he ordered him put into his oven and baked, and he claimed that that stopped that particular crime. But that is not the method we adopt in more civilized countries. But there is this tendency by the officials of the Department of Agriculture to make the penalties for any infraction of their rules and regulations very severe, and for that reason I should like to see the regulations framed by the house and not by officials only.
I also notice that the explanatory note, in setting out why this legislation should be passed, says that the grade standards for hay that were serviceable twenty-five years ago when the principal demand for baled hay was for the feeding of horses in cities need to be revised. I would point out that it is not twenty-five years ago; it dates back only to 1918, when the present grade standards for hay were established. The act was amended and thoroughly revised, and the present grades were established in 1918. Now 1918 is a good deal nearer than twenty-five years ago, and I think we might expect a little more accuracy in the explanatory note.
The explanatory note also says that baled hay was principally used up to that time for [DOT]the feeding of horses. Well, they are not going to feed motor cars with baled hay even now, and I suppose that if it was good to arrange a grade of hay for feeding horses in 1918, the relationship between hay and horses is very much the same even now.
Take one of the present grades:
_ Prime timothy shall be pure timothy, perfect in colour, sound and well cured.
That was the grade established in 1918, and is there anything wrong with that now? Has anything happened in the last fifteen years, not twenty-five, to require a change in that grade?
The minister also takes power under paragraph (c) of section 3 to prescribe the places where, and the conditions under which, hay and straw shall be inspected. Suppose I am baling my hay and straw and that I am getting a horribly low price, and I discover that it has to be inspected at a point fifteen miles away from my home or where I am baling it. That would be a very serious handicap to my doing business.
The explanatory note also says that there have been urgent requests for the repeal of the existing grades. I should like to hear where those urgent requests came from. In these days when it is so difficult to do business at all, and more difficult still to do it at even a minimum of profit, we should mark time for a while rather than introduce new regulations which, however desirable in themselves from the point of view of an official, are calculated to hinder business. Let the wretched farmer, if he can, get a sale for his baled hay and straw, and sell it under the conditions which have been in effect for the last fifteen years. I would ask the minister- I suppose he cannot speak now-to take notice of my suggestion that these regulations should be passed by the house and not be left to the officials.

The information given, the house thus far by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) has been very meagre, and I trust that before the bill passes he will amplify it somewhat.
This bill, or a somewhat modified one, should have been passed many years ago in Canada. One was introduced in 1928 or 1929, but a very much different bill, and it was opposed so strenuously by both wings of the then opposition that it was let die on the order paper. Just previous to that, a good many bills of a similar nature providing for the standardization and grading of farm products had been introduced by the then government, but the house seemed to think that we were going too rapidly in that direction. I am afraid that some of my colleagues thought the same, because they were quite satisfied to let the bill go by default, and I think maybe they were right because we were going perhaps a little rapidly. But I am glad to see that the minister is following in our footsteps, in that respect somewhat hesitantly, but nevertheless following.
As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has pointed out, this is rather an arbitrary bill, and it may seem strange that I am rather disposed to approve of it, but the bill must first be modified by explanations or otherwise in order to remove its arbitrary

Exchequer Court Act

nature. I hope the minister in his explanation will be able to satisfy the house on that point.
We have some five or six provinces which are concerned in the selling of hay, the mari-times, Quebec, parts at least of Ontario, part of Alberta, and there is a little selling in British Columbia, and then there are two other provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan which are concerned in the buying of hay. All these provinces either as sellers or buyers are interested in the grades of hay, and I would suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that he follow the example of the government of 1906, not a bad one to follow in many respects, and consult with the provincial Ministers of Agriculture in the various provinces, whether they sell hay or not, and get their views on any new classification of hay, before being adopted by the minister. I remember that in 1906 the new grades were submitted to the Department of Agriculture in Saskatchewan, and because we were consulted we got more loyally behind the bill.
It is a very' naked bill that is before us, consisting of only three sections, and a fourth section repealing the old law. It is both naked and arbitrary, and I trust that the minister will give some explanation that will satisfy us before this bill is given its second reading. Then when it goes to the committee on agriculture we shall be able to make any modifications that are thought desirable. I am not going to oppose the second reading now because of the arbitrary nature of this bill because I think that the advice which the Ministers of Agriculture of the various provinces are in a position to give will give the minister all the direction necessary and enable us to get through a simple bill which can be modified from time to time as circumstances require, and which will also avoid the necessity of bringing these grading bills too frequently before this house.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the select standing committee on agriculture and colonization.

Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 26, to amend the Exchequer Court Act.
Mr. A. R. LaVERGNE (Montmagny): Mr. Speaker, I have no objection to the principle of the bill, but I am afraid when it reaches the committee stage it will have to be amended. A part of clause (2) in the bill reads:
... the Exchequer court shall not have jurisdiction to entertain any action heretofore

or hereafter commenced for the recovery of any sum of money paid to His Majesty voluntarily in mistake of law, if the recovery of such money might not in England be the subject of a suit or action against the crown.
This would seem to put the province of Quebec under the English common law, and when the bill comes to the committee stage I think there should be an amendment so far as the civil code of the province of Quebec is concerned.

Mr. Speaker, I believe it would be better to go into committee and have the explanations at that time, because I must say I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for Montmagny (Mr. LaVergne). I should like to hear some explanation.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
On section 1-Payments made voluntarily to His Majesty in mistake of law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as is well known the
Exchequer Court of Canada was founded by a statute which is now chapter 34 of the Revised Statutes of Canada. The jurisdiction of that court is expressed in section 18 of the act as follows:
IS. The Exchequer court shall have exclusive original jurisdiction in all cases in which demand is made or relief sought in respect of any matter which might, in England, be subject of a suit or action against the crown, and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms, it shall have exclusive original jurisdiction in all cases in which the land, goods or money of the subject are in the possession of the crown, or in which the claim arises out of a contract entered intc by or on behalf of the crown.
Then section 19 sets out a specific number of cases in which the court shall have jurisdiction. As shown in section 18, the Exchequer court is founded on the law of England and, as is well known, it is a court established by federal authority and has jurisdiction throughout all parts of Canada; irrespective of provinces. The only limitation in regard to the act, so far as I am aware, is the limitation contained in section 32 which prescribes that the statutes of limitations in effect in the various provinces shall have application to all suits pending before the Exchequer court. That is the only limitation.
It so happens that from time to time claims arise against the crown for the return of moneys which have been paid under mistake of law. Sometimes when claims are made

Customs Act
in respect of taxes, customs dues or the like, and where litigation ensues or is threatened, the parties compromise their claims and payment is made on the basis of compromise with the government of Canada. It has happened that in respect of some claims which have been so paid, subsequently by a decision of a superior court in Canada or by a decision of the judicial committee of the Privy Council, the law under which the money has been paid has been declared to be ultra vires of this parliament. Claims then immediately arise from the parties who have paid the money claiming recovery back of the amounts they have so paid. It is a well known principle of British law that when money is paid in settlement of a claim or of a litigated matter, when there has been no fraud or no threat of any kind made, the money cannot be recovered back. It is a further principle of British law that money paid under a mistake of law cannot be recovered. The theory is that the parties were at arms length, and were advised by their friends or solicitors, that they compromised and that settlement was made. If money has been so paid under a law which subsequently has been declared to be ultra vires, or an improper law, that money cannot be recovered back.
The object of this amendment is to declare that in Canada, in actions or proceedings before the exchequer court, that common principle of British law shall apply throughout all parts of Canada, and that the law in that respect shall be general throughout the length and breadth of Canada. The effect would be that in all matters which come within the jurisdiction of the exchequer court no party will be able to set up a claim in that court that he should get his money back because he paid it under a mistake of law. That is the proposal contained in the bill.

Mr. Chairman, I am
sorry I have not had time to consider this bill, which was introduced only two days ago, because in my view it is very important. If I followed the explanations of the minister it would appear that this bill would not be necessary were it not for the law of the province of Quebec. After all, the Exchequer court is given jurisdiction in matters between the crown and the subjects, but it has to apply the laws of the various provinces. In the province of Quebec we have what is called repetition de 1'indu, or recovery of money paid under mistake. The proposed legislation would take away jurisdiction from the Exchequer court, and in a roundabout way apply to the province of Quebec the principle of the common law which, under the laws of the 53719-1395
province is not applied. I would ask my hon. friend to let the matter stand in order to give me and other members opportunity to consider the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I will be very glad indeed to let the matter stand. But before the committee rises I think I might point out that this proposal does not come in any way in conflict with the law of the province of Quebec within that province. There are provisions in the Quebec code under which money can be recovered when paid under mistake of law, and no one for a moment proposes to disturb that provision within the province of Quebec. But the Exchequer court is a federal court applicable to all parts of the Dominion of Canada. It is not intended in any way to disturb the operation of the law of the province of Quebec as applicable to residents of that province or to any matter which arises in that province.
However, I see that the point taken is of sufficient importance and intricacy to require some study. I would move therefore that the committee rise and report progress, and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.

Hon. E. B. RYCKMAN (Minister of National Revenue) moved the second reading of Bill No. 30 to amend the Customs Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. LaVergne in the chair.

Will the
minister explain?
Mr. RYrCKMAN: This bill deals only with procedure or administration. The explanation, of the first section is fully stated in the explanatory note. It has been found that by reason of this phrase "value for duty" not being explained and applied there is a failure under section 217 of the Customs Act. That section provides:
Where the goods so harboured, kept, concealed, purchased, sold or exchanged are of the value of two hundred dollars, or over, such person shall be guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a term of imprisonment-
The point taken, and I think, well taken, is this, that while this subsection 3 deals with value for duty, the magistrate before whom a smuggler comes, in cases of liquor, if it is specific duty say of $7 a gallon, says that there is no value for duty. That is a specific duty. Therefore the smuggler goes free; his defence is good. We desire therefore to define "value for duty" as it occurs in this act. I
Customs Act

may say that the same definition of "value for duty" appears in section 85 of the Special War Revenue Act, which says:
(b) "duty paid value" shall mean the value of the article as it would be determined for the purpose of calculating an ad valorem duty upon the importation of such article into Canada under the laws relating to the customs and the customs tariff whether such article be in fact subject to ad valorem or other duty or not, and in addition the amount of the custom duties, if any, payable thereon;
So, as hon. gentlemen will see, this is just a simple amendment to clarify the law and make those answerable to it who should properly be answerable.
Did the minister state that under the existing provisions of the act it was impossible to collect duty on an article, assuming it to be liquor, if the value is not over $200?

Evidently I have not made myself understood. Where one harbours or conceals or keeps goods contrary to the provisions of the Customs Act there is a penalty involved. No one cavils at the penalty, the point is that it refers to value for duty, and when the question of value for duty comes before the magistrate he says there is no value for duty when there is a specific duty.
Would the $200 enter in at all?

Not at all. No matter what the penalty is, it is a case of the smuggler going free because it has been held that unless "value for duty" is defined as we have it here or in some similar way, there is no value for duty; therefore, there can be no offence.
Are not the penalties higher if the goods are of a value of $200 or over?
This section deals with goods of the value of $200 or over. The penalty is less when the value is less than $200. But it is not a question of the value of the goods that comes into consideration now.
But would not the paragraph have the effect of bringing goods of a value of less than $200 under certain specific penalties?

No, I do not think so. I think this clause, which as I say is the same as we already have in our Special War Revenue Act, would define "value for duty" the ad valorem value of the article would be taken into consideration. Some of us have an idea of what the ad valorem value of

spirits may be, and I must freely admit that in determining the value under section 217 of chapter 42 that would be taken into consideration.
Would the minister read subsection 3 of section 217?

I will be glad to, but for the sake of a clearer explanation perhaps I had better read subsections 1 and 2 as well. Subsection 1 is as follows:
If any person, whether the owner or not, without lawful excuse, the proof of which shall be on the person accused, harbours, keeps, conceals, purchases, sells or exchanges any goods unlawfully imported into Canada, whether such goods are dutiable or not, or whereon the duties lawfully payable have not been paid, such goods, if found, shall be seized and forfeited without power of remission, and, if such goods are not found, the person so offending shall forfeit the value thereof without power of remission.
Subsection 2 reads:
Every such person shall, in addition to any other penalty forfeit a sum equal to the value of such goods, which may be recovered in any court of competent jurisdiction, and shall further be liable, on summary conviction before two justices of the peace, to a penalty not exceeding two hundred dollars and not less than fifty dollars, or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year and not lees than one month, or to both fine and imprisonment.
Subsection 3 reads:
Where the goods so harboured, kept, concealed, purchased, sold or exchanged are of the value of two hundred dollars, or over, such person shall be guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a term of imprisonment. . . .
As both lawyers and laymen, I think, will appreciate, the point is that it has been held that under subsection 3 of section 217 there is no value for duty when it is a specific duty. We want to correct that omission in the interests of the administration of the law. I hope this is an understandable presentation of the case.

As yet I have been unable to get the point of view of the minister. I did understand that paragraph 3 indicated that there were higher penalties for the harbouring of goods valued at over $200 than there were for harbouring goods valued at less than $200, but I do not know that the crown will improve its position by adding this definition of value for duty. The proposed section reads:
"Value for duty" means the value of the article os it would be determined for the purpose of calculating an ad valorem duty upon the importation of such article into Canada under the laws relating to the customs and the customs tariff, whether such article be in fact subject to ad valorem or other duty or not.

Customs Act
Does that mean the customs collector for that port would be called in by the prosecution in order to establish wihat would be the duty?

I would understand it
to mean that the customs appraiser would value the article in question just as it would be valued if there were an ad valorem duty payable.

The minister would not
consider repealing that section altogether, would he?

Does the minister really
think it is desirable, in fixing the penalty for a criminal offence, to make it depend upon the uncertainties of assessment by the customs appraiser? No one wants to protect an offender, but it seems to me that the offender at least ought to have some sort of notice of wihat offence he is committing and the penalty to which he may be liable. If you use as the test of whether a man is liable to the lesser or the greater penalty the value for duty as it may be fixed by the customs appraiser under the various sections of the customs act, then it seems to me you have not been quite fair to the criminal, because he does not know and cannot tell what the penalty is. He never will know, and the court will not know until somebody comes to the witness stand, takes the book and sa3's that for the purposes of duty the goods would be appraised at a certain figure, perhaps two or three times their real value. Would it not be satisfactory so far as the minister is concerned, and so far as the enforcement of the act is concerned, to adopt the same test that is adopted in subsections 1 and 2. namely the value of the goods? Then there is no trouble; anyone ought to know the value of the goods being harboured or kept, but if you adopt the uncertain test of the value for duty I do not think you are carrying out the principles which generally surround both the specification and the administration of criminal law, namely that there should be some certainty about it.
I wonder what is the objection of the minister, or if there really is any objection, to using the word "value" instead. I quite appreciate that "value for duty" has been in the act before, but while the minister is amending the act, and in view of the increased powers which have been given to fix arbitrary values, I would suggest that now is the time to let the value of the goods determine what penalty shall be imposed.

I may say to my hon.
friend that the question he has raised really
does not seem to be a proper one in view of what is proposed. This amendment is not suggested for the purpose of influencing or affecting in any way any penalty whatever. It is brought forward without regard to what the penalty may be. My hon. friend will find that the word "value" is defined in the interpretation section of the Customs Act.

Just the word "value"
alone.

Yes, and these words
"value" and "value for duty" as hon. members know have a difference in signification.
I merely ask that a man bringing in silks, for instance, on which there is an ad valorem duty, shall not be subject to these penalties while a man who brings in liquor, to refer to the commodity I mentioned before, gets off because there is a specific duty on that article. \Ve want to put everyone on the same footing, and there is nothing in the suggested amendment except equal treatment for all. It will be seen from the interpretation we place on "value for duty" that it is the actual value of the article, which should be known by the importer.
Not the actual value.

I quote from the
amendment:
"Value for duty" means the value of the article as it would be determined for the purpose of calculating an ad valorem duty.
It seems to me there can be no objection to that when our customs tariff has both ad valorem and specific duties. If a man is found harbouring and concealing goods to cheat the customs, in the one case he would be subject to a penalty and not in the other because of the technical interpretation made by magistrates as to the value for duty. That is what we wish t'o correct.

I do not think the minister understands what I am suggesting. I am saying that there should be absolute equality with regard to goods upon which an ad valorem duty is imposed and those upon which a specific duty is imposed. That equality can be effected by making the value of the goods the value for duty proposes in order to decide as to whether the greater or lesser penalty should be imposed. The minister might have a prosecution against a certain man for harbouring goods. How is he going to know whether or not that is an indictable offence until the customs appraiser steps into the stand and states that if the goods had been subject to an ad valorem duty he would have valued them at so much.
Customs Act
It is unfair for my hon. friend to state the ease in that way.

I do not intend to be
unfair.

My hon. friend says
that the value would not be known until the appraiser stepped into the box, but that is not the case. In order for a man to get his goods he would have to come before a customs officer, the man would be treated the same way in the one case as in the other. The man would not be brought into court without knowing what he is charged with.

The minister misses the
point. If a man was charged with harbouring goods that had been imported unlawfully, those goods would not have passed through the customs. There would be no appraisement made by a customs officer and the magistrate or the prosecuting officer would not know whether to lay the charge as an indictable or summary offence. The customs officer would have to be called to fix the value. The governor in council has power to impose all sorts of arbitrary values and a man may be charged with a more serious offence if the customs appraiser decides that the goods in question shall be valued at so much for duty purposes. When a man harbours silks or other similar goods he knows what the value is; if they are worth more than $200 he knows that he will be liable to the greater penalty. However, in the case of many other commodities he might be liable only to the lesser penalty. I am suggesting that it should be made equitable all round, it should be the same in this subsection as it is in subsections 1 and 2.

If what my hon. friend states is an injustice, it has existed in every case where an ad valorem duty is applied. I have never heard of it having worked unfairly and no complaints have been made against it. We are simply putting the two men upon the same footing and not making it subject to a magistrate's interpretation of the value for duty. Everyone who is familiar with the workings of the Customs Act knows that there is a right of appeal. If one is bent upon asserting his rights he has abundant opportunity to do so. We are simply trying to place those guilty of infractions of the law upon the same footing as far as ad valorem and specific duties are concerned.

I am sorry the former Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) is not in the chamber as he might recall with me that at the time this act was passed there was a somewhat bitter ntroversy in the house. 
It was contended that this was too arbitrary a power to place in the hands of the customs department, and that we had not really met the distinction between commercial smuggling and the ordinary petty smuggling which goes on over the border every day where people who have entered the United States come back with a pair of silk stockings or two or three packages of cigarettes. As I recall it, the debate at that time lasted through two or three sittings of the house. As the hon. member for Waterloo is not present, perhaps I should not refer to the fact that the bill was finally passed on a Friday night when most of the members who had opposed it were away. At that time an arbitrary power was given to the customs department; that was bad, but this is far worse. As the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) has pointed out, it would be impossible to know the value of the goods being harboured or smuggled until such time as a customs officer came into the box and stated that the particular merchandise was worth so much. In many cases 'he might not know himself until he had consulted with the higher officials of the department. If the articles harboured, hidden or smuggled were not articles usually imported in the ordinary course of business, I have not the slightest doubt but that the customs officer would have to apply to the commissioner of customs to find out what value had been placed upon them for duty purposes. I submit to the minister that it would be in the interests of the crown itself in avoiding expense in the prosecutions, and it would certainly be fairer to everyone if he would say that the value to be taken into consideration in the prosecution Shall be the real value of the article. He does not require the other sections of the Customs Act for the purposes of prosecution.

Let me interrupt for a
moment. That is exactly what this amendment proposes. The subsection reads:
"Value for duty" means the value of the article as it would be determined for the purpose of calculating an ad valorem duty upon the importation of such article into Canada under the laws relating to the customs and customs tariff, whether such article be in fact subject to ad valorem or other duty or not.

"Under the laws relating to the customs and customs tariff." The laws relating to the customs and customs tariff provide that there may be an arbitrary valuation for duty purposes, a valuation which cannot possibly be known to the person accused of this offence.

I submit that the section absolutely excludes an arbitrary value.

Customs Act

My hon. friend suggested
that I was unfair; I do not think that that statement is quite fair. The section reads: "Value for duty" means the value of the article as it would be determined for the purpose of calculating an ad valorem duty upon the importation of such article into Canada

We want to put them
both upon the same footing.

My hon. friend suggests
that that means the actual value. I think I could ask any importer to step into the witness box to deny that the value for duty purposes is the actual value of the goods, and particularly the value for duty as it would be determined. There have to be two presumptions; there has to be the presumption that the goods are subject to an ad valorem duty, which they are not, and there has to be the presumption that they are worth a certain amount which the appraiser is going to fix, which they are not. That is the sort of thing upon which the prosecution, the conviction and the punishment is going to be based. My hon. friend says that this has been done in the past; it is quite true that it was done in the past but at that time the value for duty meant the fair market value and only in the case of manufactured goods, under a special provision, was there any permission to make an arbitrary value. That has all gone by the board in the legislation of the last three years, and now my hon. friend and his officials have a right to fix any value under the sun-[DOT]
That is not correct.

-and to call that the value for duty purposes. My hon. friend proposes to rest a criminal prosecution and punishment on that. I cannot see, and with all due deference to him I do not think he can see any reason that the real value of the goods should not be the test whether the increased penalty should be imposed. That would be putting the section squarely in line with the two previous ones, and he would not then be permitting an arbitrary prosecution based on an arbitrary price.
Is it not a question of value in each case?
No, a question of guess.
The only objection I take is that if the act is not to be amended for the honest importer, then we shall be giving a preference to the man who is trying to evade the law.

Let us take this case. How much is a gallon of alcohol worth? For ready reckoning, let us call it fifty cents.
The value of that alcohol, after it is free of customs, is much more than that. The tax which we impose is $7 a gallon. Supposing there were twenty gallons; that would mean SI40 in value of duty. But if the actual value is to be taken, then you would find our friends asking that fifty cents should be used and the total would be $10. Everyone knows twenty gallons of spirits, if it is potable, is worth more than $10, and thus one can see the justice in appraising the value of the article.
There has been no trouble in the administration of this section. What the hon. member for Quebec South says is true, not however, with regard to section 217. As far as I understand the matter, there was no complaint made against this section. I think I may fairly put it in this way: as one offender comes under the law and another, on account of a technicality, does not, would it not be proper to make the law cover all actual offences, putting one man on the same footing as another? That is what we are trying to do. We have a value for duty in terms of the Special War Revenue Act. This is just to make the law fairly applicable.

WTe know in the last few years powers have been given to the minister to fix on goods coming into Canada any value he likes, regardless entirely of what the goods are actually worth. We know, if a man is found with goods in his possession of the actual value of $100. that have been imported without paying duty, that man is liable to a certain penalty. We know if he is found with goods of the value of S200 on which duty has not been paid, he is liable to a much heavier penalty. The provision of this clause, as I understand it, will put in the hands of the minister's officials power to value these goods so that the duty to be paid will be higher and the man will suffer a greater penalty. He may be in possession of goods of the actual value of $100, but the customs official can go into court and say: I value those goods at $200, and in that way the penalty will be much heavier.
He cannot do that.
That is the lacv as I understand it. There are lawyers in the house who will put the same interpretation on it. If it is not so, will the minister so state definitely?

What my hon. friend has said about the law and the facility with which customs appraisers can act, is altogether incorrect.
Customs Act

Will my hon. friend state, as a fact with respect to goods imported honestly and fairly, on which duty has been paid, that a customs appraiser cannot, on instructions and under powers vested in the minister, put any value he likes on those goods?
I will state positively that he cannot do so.
- There are unfortunately many people who have paid duties who say otherwise.
They have not paid duty on any value, no matter what it might be, that the minister cared to fix.
That is the sort of stuff hon. members opposite have broadcast through the country.
Not at all. I am not prepared to stand for that. I am ready to bring the evidence before the house.
Bring it in.
Let me put a concrete case. The Prime Minister announced, during the time we were putting through the Economic conference agreements-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The opposition were not putting them through; they opposed them.

The right hon. gentleman mentioned wire; he said that wire was coming from Holland at a certain price and that it was not allowed to come into Canada at the price suggested. The Minister of National Revenue being vested with the right, for duty purposes placed an arbitrary value on barbed wire. Is that so?
No.
What did the hon. gentleman do?
Exercised his intelligence. That is all.
How did he keep out the wire?

What was found was this, that a German concern which was manufacturing barbed wire, was shipping it to be barbed in Holland because barbed wire was not in common use there, in order that it might in a country where there was no real market, establish a price which was a dumping and unfair price. It was shown that in Germany where this company had their home, they were charging more for barbed wire. It was shown that in Belgium, lying just alongside, they charged less for 
it, but they went to Holland where barbed wire was not in extensive use and when called upon to say how much was used there, they said 6,500 tons. It turned out that part of that was re-exported from the country. They were trying to establish a price to ruin anyone engaged in the business in Canada, and under section 36, not by action immediately of the minister, a value was fixed for barbed wire. What would have been the result if this barbed wire which it was proposed to distribute here, had been allowed to enter Canada? There would have been no chance of doing business in this country by the companies already here and the result would have been that later people would have paid through the nose, prices they never paid before, for barbed wire.

Does the same principle apply, as regards the valuation for duty purposes, to all articles? Under the old dumping act, if anyone attempted to sell goods cheaper in Canada than in the country of origin, the dumping duty applied. Will the minister say whether the same principle applies in regard to the valuation of goods coming into Canada to-day?

I shall say that dumping does not in any sense apply in the consideration of the amendment now before us. If my hon. friend desires me to answer any question arising out of his own knowledge of any particular subject, I should be glad to sit down with him and discuss it, and I am sure that he will find that there is no enlarged power taken of fixation. It is already provided under section 36 of the Customs Act what action shall be taken by the department itself, irrespective of the minister or the government, and such action is taken in the ordinary routine of the department. Yet members rise in the house and tell us that there has been some fixation by the minister of outlandish prices. I can only stress as emphatically as I can that such is not the case.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Might I say one word in answer to my hon. friend from South Battle-ford? The question of valuation was always predicated upon what was described as fair market value in the country of origin; that is, the price that would be paid in normal trading transactions for the commodity in question.
Except there is a distress market.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I said fair market value. Distress market has nothing to do with it;
I am leaving that out altogether. The difficulty arose because the surplus product of foreign manufactures was thrown upon the

Customs Act
Canadian and other markets at prices which were less than the fair market value. If any of the members of the committee are disposed to read the speech that Mr. Fielding made upon the matter when section 43 was introduced into our statutes by the late Senator Bureau, they will realize just what the difficulties in this country were. The fair market value became almost impossible to determine for many, many reasons, and we had what was called a dumping duty, but that was found to be wholly inadequate to meet the situation, and the extraordinary provision of the act of 1930-31-

Extraordinary is a good
word.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, to save the industrial structure of Canada.
And ruin its farmers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It did not. It saved the entire fruit industry, and I challenge the hon. gentleman to point to a single injury to any farmer by reason of it.
How about barbed wire?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Barbed wire did not do
any injury, but the price of barbed wire was not enhanced by reason of any action that was taken.
The price was maintained.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Certainly it was, and I
explained to the house when I was asked questions about barbed wire just what the situation was, that I do not think any member of this house believes in his own mind that it is sound business for Canadians to permit any commodity to displace Canadian commodities at distress prices, with the effect of destroying the Canadian industry, and then leaving the Canadian consumers subject to the price of a monopoly. That is what it gets down to. You must at least take a view of these matters beyond the immediate day. I could name half a dozen instances, if it rvere relevant to this particular matter, in which what I have indicated actually happened. It is a question that is not in the realm of doubt or conjecture; it is a real happening. Now Canada, we hope, will endure beyond to-day and to-morrow, but if your policies are based solely upon to-day, then the result is that to-morrow you suffer, and I wonder if there is anything clearer than the example of the railways in Canada on that point.
I hope my hon. friend is not blaming the dumping duties for ruining the railways.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The same principle.
Everybody was clamouring for railways. Democracy got railways, and the day after woke up and discovered that it had destroyed itself. That is what happens in regard to these commodities.
Other things hapnened to the railways too.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I will admit that. The hon. gentleman managed them for seven or eight years politically.
We will discuss that when the railways are up.
The railways were carrying goods then.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, they were carrying loans.
What are they carrying now?
Deficits.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: When the hon. gentlemen have exhausted themselves, I shall proceed. Fair market value was the test that was imposed, and when the fair market value could not be ascertained, other means were resorted to, to ascertain what that fair market value was, and the duties payable have been the duties payable on fair market value with fair competition. Hon. gentlemen no doubt saw in this morning's paper that yesterday the president of the Board of Trade in England said that England would have to take steps to save her shipping from unfair competition.
More navigation laws.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has suggested one method by which it could be done.
Going back a hundred years.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has discovered that one hundred years of experience has taught lessons.
I think three years have taught some.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The people of this country have discovered that unless the steps taken had been taken there would have been no industrial fabric left in Canada.
The point at issue in this bill is one which the minister explained very clearly, and I cannot understand why there is all the fuss about it. You could not convict for violation of the statute because the duty payable on importation was in specific terms rather than in ad valorem terms, and that made possible punishment for a violation of the law. What the value is, is a matter of evidence. It always is. That is a matter of procedure
Customs Act

and evidence; that is all. The evidence will establish the value, and when the value is established, that is all there is to it; the duty then attaches at the rate indicated. Is there anything very strange about that? I cannot see it. Of course, I am open to conviction always.
The Prime Minister is improving.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is amazing what adversity does. If the hon. gentleman had to carry the burden of responsibility that I have done for the last three years, he probably would have improved too. I realize more and more every day what are the conditions in this country and the burdens we have to carry, and I endeavour to adapt myself as best I may to the continuance of the burden. I am grateful to the hon. gentleman if he thinks I show signs of improvement, for I should hesitate to remain, in the words of Pitt, one of those who continue ignorant despite the warnings of age and experience. That is all there is in this legislation, and I suggest it might be a reasonable thing to adopt it so that those who have violated the law in the past shall not be able to escape on a technicality.

I have not the statute before me, but speaking from memory, the 1930 amendments to the Customs Aot give the minister power to fix valuation for duty, and he would fix those values for duty according to the price the Canadian producer thought he should get. I think the statute provides for a minimum price, that the price so fixed shall not be less than the cost of production plus profit to the manufacturer in the country of origin. That was the minimum, and the sky was the maximum. There is nothing in the statute as it now stands to prevent them making any valuation they like. Mention has been made of barbed wire. Will the minister tell us whether or not any confidential letters have been sent out from the department to the customs collectors in regard to valuation for barbed wire?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think that question is relevant to the matter before the chair.

I shall be very glad to answer if the chairman will allow me. I know of no such letters. Any letters that would be sent out would be in the ordinary routine of the office, and barbed wire would not be dealt, with any differently from any other commodities coming under the direction of the department. I know of no such letters.

If the minister knows of no such letter in regard to barbed wire, will he tell us if any confidential letters have been sent out by the department touching valuation for duty? Have those letters been sent out tor the purpose of fixing the values for duty without allowing the importer to know the value until he has to pay the duty?
I know of no such instance.
I should like to ask the minister if in the application of these changes he intends to use the Royal Canadian Mounted Police?

I do not know that that point comes under consideration in the discussion of these amendments, but as the hon. member knows, what is called the preventive service is now under the control of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Part of it still remains with the Department of National Revenue, that part which might be termed the investigation branch. Investigations come peculiarly within the Department of National Revenue. But it was thought that where there was protective work to be done and enforcement of the law to be carried out, that in view of the fact that we had a police force which does its work efficiently that force should do the work formerly done by the Department of National Revenue.

I am assuming a great part of the work of the Department of Customs will be undertaken by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I should like to state to the minister the fact that in this case, as in many others, there will be overlapping of jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I believe the hon.
member is out of order. Unless there is general consent the preventive service cannot be discussed at this time.

I am quite willing to
answer any question the hon. member may ask. However, as you have said, Mr. Chairman, this does not seem to be the proper time to discuss the preventive service. When my estimates are before the committee I shall be happy to answer any question which may arise. If the hon. member finds it impossible to be in the house at that time, and will be good enough to let me have a memorandum of the information he desires, I shall be very happy to reply.

I am prepared to wait and ask my question at another time. There is a specific occurrence in mind, however,

Customs Act
which I should like to bring to the attention of the house, one which took place in my constituency only last week. I am satisfied, however, to wait until later.

How
many cases were dismissed under the old section? There is reference made to these prosecutions under the explanatory note.

I cannot tell my hon.
friend. I must say, however, there was more than one shot, and we thought we had to mend our fences.

In all
the provinces?

I cannot tell my hon.
friend, but I shall inquire and let him know.

I may be
dense, but I do not yet understand the situation. We will suppose someone attempts, to import two gallons of liquor into the country, knowing perfectly well that he is evading the customs law to the extent of $14, or at the rate of $7 per gallon. When he is caught and apprehended it is very easy to ascertain the amount he owes customs authorities. In addition, however, there is a desire to punish him. Are there no penalties in the act for infractions, without fixing values, or is this change merely for the purpose of fixing the amount of penalty? We will say, for example, that the reason for the insertion of the $200 means that if it is under $200 a magistrate cannot impose a penalty as severe as it would be if it were over $200. Is that where the difference arises?

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the hon. member's question. If he had sectiion 217 of the Customs Act before him he would find that where the value is small the party is liable on summary conviction before a justice to a penalty not exceeding $200 and not less than $50, or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year and not less than one month, or to both fine and imprisonment. But where the amount involved is larger, as stated in subsection 3 of section 217, there is an indication that the offenders have been indulging in what we call commercial smuggling, or that they are making a business of it. There is an indication that they are harbouring and concealing, in an extensive way, in contravention of the customs law. In the office we call that commercial smuggling, and the commercial smuggler receives more severe treatment than the one who may smuggle a small amount of alcohol for his own benefit or for the purpose of having a celebration with his friends. Only a day or
two ago there was an instance where twenty-four men held a celebration; true, under the law they were committing a breach of the Exoise Act, under which the penalties are more extreme. It is our hope that at this session those penalties may be modified. The twenty-four of them signed a round-robin stating they were all guilty, not knowing that they were making themselves liable to a fine of $200 and one month in gaol. That was not a case of commercial smuggling. The magnitude of the offence is something which must be considered, because in one case it is setting the law at naught, but in the other it is not only setting the law at naught but trying to make money out of doing so.

Mr. Chairman, the minister
has stated there have been no cases of extreme valuation placed on goods. I should like to give him the circumstances of a case which came under my notice not long ago. A man without money settled on a homestead in southern Saskatchewan close to the Montana border. He managed to get a little lumber with which to build a Shack; he had no furniture. A neighbour living across the line, on the American side, gave him an old democrat, from the body of which he made a cupboard. Another neighbour sold him the remains of an old mower for the sum of $5. With that purchase, added to other parts he was able to pick up, he made himself a mower sufficient for his purposes. His total investment was $5. These articles which were gathered from his neighbours' junk heaps were reported to customs officials, one of whom came along and put a valuation of about $40 on the goods. The farmer was told that the value for duty would be that amount. If that is not extreme valuation, I do not know what could be; it is both arbitrary and extreme. It might easily have happened that the customs collector would not have come along until the farmer had gathered a little more junk from his neighbours, at which time the valuation might have been placed higher than $200. Under those circumstances the farmer would have found himself liable under the criminal code. I say the valuations put on are absurd.

I had not heard of the
circumstances to which the hon. member has referred, but I believe they have no relation whatever to the clause we are now discussing.

It shows exactly to what extent criminal law is being carried, when it is suggested that the penalty shall be based on a valuation of that kind. That is exactly what my hon. friend was endeavouring to point out. I understand the suggestion has been made that we have no arbitrary duties.
Customs Act

All of us have been giving examples in this house right along of the most arbitrary duties being imposed. We started out by saying we were going to have dumping duties, imposed in this way, that the customs appraiser was going to value the goods at the amount at which they would sell in the country of origin, that was to be the test. We soon got beyond that, we said:	No we will
not pay much attention to the selling price in the country of origin if it is below the cost of production in Canada; we will increase those values to meet at least the cost of production in Canada. That did not go far enough; then we abandoned any rule whatever, and gave the customs officer the right to put on any value he likes. Those arbitrary duties are being imposed from day to day. I think if my hon. friend reads the mail of his department he will find that complaints are coming every day from importers who if they place an order for delivery three months later have no idea whatever how much duty they are going to have to pay, owing to such arbitrary valuations. And that is to be the basis of criminal prosecutions launched against citizens of this country for harbouring. My hon. friend is always talking of spirituous liquors, as if they were the only thing on which specific duty is imposed. Let us take socks, upon which there is a specific duty. A man can have a bale of them in his cellar; he knows what the penalty is. But a, customs officer is found who says:	If I
had to determine the value of these goods for duty purposes, instead of $10 I would have valued them at $50, or instead of $100 I would have valued them at $300. A man incurs a penalty simply on the decision of the customs officer. Our objection is based on the fact that these arbitrary duties are being constantly imposed. Value for duty means something entirely different from what it meant when this provision of the law came into force; then it was fair market value, now it is any value the appraiser sees fit to put on.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot
let the remark of my hon. friend go without an answer. I tell him specifically across the floor of this house that when he says the minister has the power to fix any duty he likes-those are his words as I caught them-
Valuation.
-I say that is untrue. I will also add that the legislation that is upon the statute books, with the exception of the amendment made to section 43, was put od the statute books by the party opposite.

Oh, no. If my hon. friend will read the sections of the act from No. 35 on, he will find the minister has that power. He will find further that the governor in council can give the minister special power. He will find that the only arbitrary power given under the former act was the power with respect to natural products and nothing else. That has now been extended to cover all the commodities we import into Canada.
Section agreed to on division.
On section 2-Special permission for lightening vessel and unlading goods.

Just a word in explanation. Section 8 of the Customs Act says that we shall not work on Sundays and statutory holidays nor between sunset and sunrise. That has been the law for a long time. As my hon. friends must of course know, it is sometimes necessary-not desirable but necessary-to work on a holiday. It is sometimes desirable to work between sunset and sunrise. We want that privilege in exceptional cases and when the minister authorizes that the work shall be done. As mentioned in the explanatory note, there was one case where not being allowed to lighter a boat resulted in an expense of about $2,500. Some of these boats cannot approach the wharf without being lightened, and it is necessary sometimes to do that when otherwise we would like to be at our devotions or taking our ease. I think the amendment is reasonable and should commend itself to the committee.
I do not think the explanation justifies the change as far as working on Sundays is concerned.
Hear, hear.

Doubtless it is possible that some company or corporation or individual may lose as much as $2,500 by not working on Sundays, but that happens everywhere and in every sphere. All the big corporations are losing more than that by being obliged not to work on Sundays. How will my hon. friend reconcile this legislation with the Lord's Day Act? He will have to amend the Lord's Day Act too, because here is the only exception covered in the Lord's Day Act as to loading and unloading of vessels. It is in chapter 123, section 11 (1):
Loading, unloading and operating any oceangoing vessel which otherwise would be unduly delayed after her scheduled time of sailing, or any vessel which otherwise would be in imminent danger of being stopped by the closing of navigation-

Supply-Dejence-Cadet Services
I do not see why there should be special privilege for unloading vessels on Sundays because of loss of money incurred by somebody by reason of having to wait until Monday. I think it is setting a bad example. And, Mr. Chairman, may I call your attention to the fact that already the law for the observance of Sunday is sometimes broken, I know that there have been many complaints in my own province about it. This is no time for the government to introduce legislation of this kind.

My hon. friend is quite satisfied to have our railway trains travel on Sunday, he is quite satisfied to sail down the St. Lawrence on Sunday. Where, because of her heavy draught, it is necessary to unload a boat to a degree before permitting her to approach a wharf, surely it is in the spirit of keeping the Lord's Day that that necessary work should be done. Provision is sought for nothing but what is necessary, and I leave it to the common sense of members of the house. Would it not be altogether reasonable that in the cases mentioned there should be opportunity, not to turn the day into a working day, but where there are special reasons for the work being done, to save it from being a breach of Sabbath observance?

I think the point taken by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) is well taken. I do not want to add to what he has said, but I think it is inadvisable to set such an example, more especially in our province where I know some friends of the party opposite are taking the provincial government to task because in some cases they have had to carry on certain impending and necessary works on Sunday. After all this is only a question of dealing with customs and excise enforcement, levying fines and so on, and I do not think these matters are of such tremendous importance that we should do away with the Lord's Day Act just to give certain officials power that may force them to break a statutory law. I do not think it ought to be done, and if this question comes to a vote I for one will vote against it.

Mr. Chairman, some
members of the committee may wish to consider this matter further, so I would move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: With the consent of the house, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by Mr. Ryckman, that we revert to the order of motions.
Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
On behalf of the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) I desire to lay on the table a partial return of correspondence with Mr. G. G. Serkau in connection with the proposed exchange of Canadian cattle for Russian goods, in response to the motion made by the hon. member for South Batlleford (Mr. Vallanee).
. SUPPLY

The house in committee of supply, Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton South) in the chair.
Militia services: cadet services, $300,000. Hon. DONALD M. SUTHERLAND (Minister of National Defence):	When the committee rose the other night we were considering this item, but since the hon. member who moved an amendment and the other hon. gentleman who said he wished to speak on the matter are not here, perhaps we might let this item stand for the time being and proceed to something else.

I would like a little information on this item, and perhaps the minister would go on with it as far as possible. If the others are not here a little later perhaps it might stand. Would that be satisfactory?
Quite so.

I wonder if the minister
would give us the number of cadet corps now operating, and also tell us if there have been any increases or decreases in the last year.

There were 1,174
corps in existence on December 31, 1932. Up to March 7 last ten new detachments had been authorized, and since that time no further authorizations have been made. Last year forty-four detachments were disbanded.

How many detachments
are there in the province of Quebec?

There are 324 corps
in Quebec.

In view of the debate which took place when this item was under consideration previously, during which members on this side of the house belonging to both the official opposition and the group in the comer gave many reasons why this amount should be reduced, I should like to. know from the minister if he has considered the advisability of reducing this vote or, if

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
that cannot be done this year, of undertaking that next year we will not be asked to pass a similar vote.
I think I am quite safe in giving that undertaking, which I gave the right hon. leader of the opposition previously. Undoubtedly the estimate next year will be very considerably reduced.
I presume the minister has no idea of the extent of that reduction.
I cannot give a definite figure, but certainly it .will be very much reduced.

I understand that when this item was under consideration the minister felt that he was hampered to some extent by existing arrangements or agreements. Let me point out to the minister that as I understand it-and he will correct me if I am wrong-the arrangements really are only with respect to the Strathcona trust fund, which really was the commencement of the cadet movement. That has to do only with the expenditure of the interest on a certain amount of money which was provided by Lord Strathcona. So far as I know there are no arrangements in the sense of contractual obligations of any kind with the provinces with regard to the expenditure of any sum such as this. understand it, we are now discussing item 84, whereby the administration seeks $300,000 for

cadet services, a reduction of $60,000 over the vote of last year. The other evening the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) explained just why this vote of $300,000 for cadet services was being asked for. At the outset of my remarks may I say that for the years which it has been my privilege and great honour to be a member of this house, I have consistently supported this vote. I am quite prepared to -accept the explanation given the other evening by the Prime Minister, to be found on pages 2114 and 2115 of Hansard. I think this explanation can be summed up in the following words of the Prime Minister:
In view of what has taken place in the past it would not be my judgment that the minister could ask the school districts to take a certain course. They are masters of the situation, they determine whether or not they will make any expenditure. At lien they determine that they will not, our obligation ceases.
I think this statement should be coupled with the statement made by the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) which appears on page 2115 of Hansard, as follows:
As has been pointed out. ten per cent is being deducted from the salaries of civil servants and economies of every kind are being attempted if not in fact practised.
And again on page 2,120:
T say to the hon. gentleman that, unless as minister of the department he wall give us an undertaking, or, unless the Prime Minister will give us an undertaking on behalf of the government, that the government is prepared to communicate with the provinces, municipalities or with whatever bodies they may have made commitments, expressing the hope that those bodies may see their way clear to forego further grants for the period of a year, I shall when it next comes lip oppose the vote for this service.
These statements show just exactly how this vote was placed before the committee.
With what my right hon. leader said I
am in absolute accord, but at the same time may I say that in my opinion in years gone by there has been very much in fact, too much, lopping off or cutting or doing away in connection with our national services. Canada has reached a stage where every bit of her national services should be preserved.
I have seen with great regret the decrease of estimates in the very essential services. It is true that this is due to circumstances, but we should not, in time of crisis, do anything that may endanger the machinery whereby the national development of Canada is brought forward, so that when times return to normal we shall not be so far away from the well-beaten path, that we shall be unable to recognize the old blazes on tihe old trees, and find the trail we then travelled in ease, luxury and happiness.
I am altogether in favour of this vote for the cadet service. It does not make very much difference to me whether there is anything military in the training which these young boys receive. I am quite sure theTe is no military training in what is given to the Boy Scouts and Girl Guides. I am confident that if at the outset of the great war, Sir Sam Hughes was able in so short a time to gather together 35,000 men, send them overseas and have them on the field of battle, it was because of the training and discipline they had received in the summer training camps. It did not make militarists out of them. I honestly believe that the many feats of valour and glory on the fields of Flanders, Ahmy, Courcellette and elsewhere had their origin in the discipline and training our youths had received in the training camps of Canada. When they found themselves in difficulty, they knew exactly wlhat to do in cases of emergency. I am not one who believes in armaments or whose maxim is, si vis pacem, para bellum, but I believe the youth of to-day, the boys and girls, would spend their time very much better in the open, in the fields, in discipline and practice, whether they use a rifle or one of those sticks with a signal flag on the end of it, than by going to moving picture houses where they receive nothing that will improve either their morals or their physique.
I wonder if the work, for instance, of the Royal Military College may be said to inculcate militarism in the minds and souls of the young men who have been fortunate enough to follow the courses given there. Those who are opposed to this training ought to look into the matter and see how many of the young men who have received their training at the Royal Military College, or, for that

Supply-Defence-Cadet Services
matter, at any other military college that exists in Canada, go about preaching warfare. A large proportion of them are following ordinary vocations in life as engineers and in other capacities. I do not for one moment think this training is conducive to the creation in the youth of to-day of a spirit which may be anti-pacifist or bellicose. Canada in her youth should be prepared for to-morrow; the youth of to-day should receive training along the lines of the old Roman and Greek physical culture. We all know in the old days the Romans and Greeks believed in "mens sana in corpore sano," a sound mind in a sound body. The mere fact that boys drill under a military system, bow to discipline, even carry muskets, will not create in their souls a desire to kill somebody else. Our policy should be based on modern methods, on the necessity of keeping in touch with present conditions, and in some way we should put a stop to this lopping off of services that are conducive to the national standard of living. By the statute of Westminster Canada is now a nation. She should be garbed in the dress or uniform that befits her to-day-long enough to cover the subject and short enough to be interesting-but please do not make it any shorter. Methinks we can not afford to lop off any more.
I am in favour of this appropriation; I shall vote against the amendment. I would be much more at ease if the minister would say that he will procure, as my right hon. leader has suggested, an undertaking that some of these schools or bodies or corporations with whom we are concerned will advise the government that they will not ask for any further grants pending the betterment of financial conditions. But if that cannot be done, then, with less gladness of heart I shall nevertheless vote for this item.

May I ask the minister whether this is under a separate administration? This might be one way in which a saving could be made. I am strongly in favour of this training and will support it in every way, but I think at the present time we are a little top-heavy, and if this administration is not separate and apart, I see no reason why the duties should not be combined with those of some part of the administrative body.

The cadet movement has developed very rapidly in the years since the war. During the last few years particularly it has gone forward by leaps and bounds, and undoubtedly if the grants were not cut down there would be a continual increase in the movement. In view of that fact and the general opinion in favour of the move-
ment, it was considered too big to be tied to any of the other departments. Under present circumstances there is a good deal in what the hon. gentleman says, and no doubt considerable changes along the line of overhead can be made.

I see no reason why the officer in charge of cadet services should not perhaps take on some other duty, thereby reducing the headquarters expenditure. On the other hand, it would be rather difficult to reduce the amount allowed for stenographers, because the officer has found it impossible to take a lady stenographer around with him to the different training classes. He insists on a male stenographer, which, of course, increases the stenographic expense. I think his reason is sound, but it makes the expenses for that section slightly higher than in the past. I repeat, however, that I can see no reason why in these days the cadet officer could not take on some other duties in order to reduce the overhead expense, especially when the whole service is being reduced.

I appreciate very much the cadet service and personally I favour the training that is given and the way it is being handled throughout Canada, But the minister stated the other night that it was impossible to reduce this vote because of commitments already made, and he went on to say that he could not promise to reduce it another year because it was outside of his jurisdiction.
I did not say that.

If that were so there would not be much use in our discussing the item.
I am exceedingly pleased that since then the minister has changed his position and now undertakes to do his best to make a reduction next year. I personally favour this vote, but in view of the conditions of the country to-day and the reductions in expenditures that are being made in all directions, I think this is one item in which we could make a substantial saving. I would make this suggestion to the minister. The fiscal year ends on March 31, and out of this vote there will be required an amount sufficient to cover only the remainder of the school year, that is, the months of April and May and up until about the middle of June. It would seem to me, therefore, that it would be an easy matter to cut this vote, as only two and a half months of the school year have to be provided for. Nearly all our schools in Canada close by the eighteenth or the twentieth of June at the latest.

The money that is being voted here?

but I am talking about a temporary holiday in cadet activities until financial conditions improve. It seems to me where there are so many necessary items of public expenditure, and where there is so much need and want and misery and suffering, this is one of the places where we could save money.

Mr. Speaker, a number of observations made in the house during the course of this debate prompts me to rise to lay my views before parliament. It has been claimed by some hon. members that in the opinions we express in this corner we do not at times represent the organized labour movement in Canada. On this occasion, however, in the few observations I intend making on this particular bill, I think 1 fairly adequately express the viewpoint of the organized labour movement. Another reason that prompts me to rise at this time is that I represent in this parliament a constituency which is probably one of the strongest from the standpoint of the communist party. In that constituency, North Winnipeg, there is what I woidd call the real centre of the' organized communist movement; from there they spread their tentacles in all directions. Therefore, if I speak on this question, I do so from a certain knowledge of the work and activities of the communist organization which has been discussed at such length in different sections of the house.
Before doing so, however, it may be as well that I refer to the fact that the legislation now before us arises from the circumstance that in 1918 a number of orders in council were passed and certain repressive measures were taken by the then government. Amongst the orders in council that were passed were those that made illegal in Canada certain organizations such as the Chinese Nationalist League, the old Social Democratic party and a number of similar organizations. Those who look back over the years and think of the action of the government of that day in repressing by law the activities of those associations will surely come to the conclusion that that action was most unwise.
But during the course of the present debate I could not help coming to the conclusion that many hon. members who have spoken have over-emphasized the importance of the communist party in this country; it has been receiving gratuitous advertising and has had thrust upon it glory and honour which it does not deserve. Canada is certainly in no danger from anything the communist party might, do or even attempt to do. In fact, I believe we have a much greater danger to fear from the stand-patters than from the communist party. I happen to know something about its strength, because for a number of years
