In Winnipeg, where I said at the outset it is probably as strong as anywhere else in Canada, if I put its number down at about 3.500 to 4.000, I am giving it a fairly generous measure for the amount of support it has in that city. That figure has been tested out in a number of elections, and even as late as November last in the mayoralty contest in Winnipeg, when they named a candidate for mayor, their votes on that occasion amounted to approximately 3.500.
In addition to the numerical strength of the communist party, they 'have a certain amount of financial strength. As to that I must confess that I have not the faintest idea where they get all the funds of which they are possessed. Only recently in Winnipeg, when about twenty of their associates were committed for trial on a charge of rioting, they were able to place in the courts of that city the sum of $20,000 in cash as bail for those individuals. Where they got that money I really cannot say.
In addition to their financial strength they are possessed of many buildings in various parts of the dominion, and again I do not know where they obtained the funds to purchase those buildings. In my constituency they must own about six different buildings where they hold their meetings, where they gather together, where they have social events, and those buildings are usually paid for and maintained out of funds owned and controlled by the organization.
As regards section 98 of the criminal code, the real opposition of the communist party to this section in my opinion is the fact that it contains one clause which was elaborated upon yesterday by the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and which gives to the government the right to confiscate property in case of its being owned or controlled by illegal organizations. The real attack of the communist party against the whole of section 98 is not against that clause which infringes upon the right of free speech or of .assembly, but against that clause Which they feel might be invoked against them and whereby they might lose the property which to-day is nominally or actually in their possession.
Efforts have been made in the house by certain hon. members who, I think, ought to know better, and who, if they do not, ought to try to understand a little more about the matter, to link us in the labour party up
with the work and activities of the communist party in Canada. It seems to me that those members have a very hazy understanding of some of our problems and of the meaning of the word "communist," and a similar hazy understanding of even the term "socialism" or the things for which we in the labour party stand. Fortunately or otherwise the term "communism" in the year 1933 has taken upon itself something of the character of those activities engaged in by the communist party in those countries where communism happens to be in operation. Now the only part of the world where the communist party is in the saddle to-day happens to be Russia, and so any action taken there by the powers that be becomes, so to speak, part and parcel of what some people like to call the activities of the communist party. On the other hand When we speak of anarchism we immediately confuse that term with the activities of the man who attempts to assassinate a ruler in some part of the world, and forget about the philosophy that underlies the theory of anarchism. Those who have read some of the books of Kropotkin and other philosophical writers on the theory of anarchism can see how far removed from anarchism are the practices of those who think they are following the ideas of the writers to whom I have just referred. Unfortunately or fortunately, communism to-day implies the things that are taking place in Russia, and naturally I do not blame anyone for condemning some of the things that are taking place to-day in soviet Russia. We of the labour party are totally opposed to a great many of the things which the communist party have done and are doing at the present time in soviet Russia. We believe fundamentally in an ordered democracy. We are opposed to all forms of dictatorship. We are opposed to a dictatorship in Moscow just as much as we are opposed to a dictatorship in Wall street. One is just as obnoxious to us as the other, and consequently when the communists in this country attempt to attack those who oppose them, their first line of attack is against those who happen to be part and parcel of the labour movement. And so in this country, as in many other parts of the world, we find those Who are closely associated with the communist party attacking those of us in this house and outside who are associated with the labour movement more vigorously than those who belong to the Liberal or the Conservative party.
In this country the. communist party has had control directly or indirectly of a number of organizations. Affiliated with them, as has

I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that we, here, of the labour party are totally opposed both to the tactics and to the ideas of the communist party as expressed in this dominion. There have been, as I said before, certain hon. members who have tried to associate us with the communist movement in Canada. I would point out to the hon. members of this house that in my last election when I was running in North Winnipeg about two and a half years ago the only districts in which I attempted to hold meetings were those in which the communists claimed to be strongest, and it was my privilege, if I call it such, at every one of those meetings to be howled down and prevented from speaking by those very people who to-day are howling for the rights of free speech in Canada.
I have no fear in the least so far as the communist party in Canada is concerned. Those who have studied British history and imbibed its traditions must realize that institutions such as parliament which have existed for about seven hundred years are not so easily going to be turned upside down by the talk and cry of a few individuals who have no knowledge of British history and of the traditions of British parliamentary institutions. In this country the strength of the communist party lies almost entirely among those of the foreign-speaking population in this dominion. It is an unfortunate fact, and one that I regret extremely. I have been in public life in this parliament or in public office for a period of over sixteen years, and during the whole of that time I have attempted to the best of my ability to do all I possibly could do to prevent racial hatreds. I have tried to bring together the component parts of our Canadian citizenship in order that we might build up a Canada that is worth while both

for ourselves and for the generations that are to come, and when I see the activities of these people who are of more recent origin in this Dominion of Canada I feel that they are not only doing a disservice to themselves but a tremendous disservice to all those people who have come to our shores during their own lifetime. I know how easy it is to stir up racial hatred in almost any part of the world. In my own constituency, comprising about 63,000 people, about forty per cent of them, or fully 25,000, are of what might be called foreign nationality, and among this 25,000 are to be found, almost exclusively, those who have come to this country from Russia. We find a section of them imbued with the idea that the only way in which improved conditions can be brought about in this dominion is by doing what has been done in Russia. The actions of this comparatively few people in Canada are having a bad effect, to my way of thinking, in a most unexpected and undesirable way. They have created amongst sections of our Canadian people a distrust and a misunderstanding of large sections of the foreign-born population of the dominion, and if some of those communists who think they are performing a useful service by their actions could only see some of the results of their activities, I am inclined to think that a great many of them would change their ways.
I have attempted to indicate the feelings of the communist party in Canada towards those of us who in some way or other have been connected with the labour movement in Canada. Those hon. members who have been attempting to link my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) with the activities of the communist party really must not have read anything that that party has had to say about the hon. member. He has been described in this house as one who is always attempting on the floor of the house to support the activities of communist organizations. I suggest that is hardly in keeping with the facts. We find that away back in 1925, when I first became a member of this chamber, we asked the then government-which was not exactly in power, but was in office-to enact certain legislation. At that time they consented, but there was nothing extraordinary in their action because prior to 1925 they took exactly the same stand as they did subsequently. Communications passed between the then Prime Minister and my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre concerning this very question. They undertook to bring in remedial measures looking towards either the amending of section 98 or its deletion from the criminal code.

There is nothing in this act which prevents a man from defending himself, from using force to defend his family or his home, but there is something in the act which prevents
2230	COMMONS
Criminal Code-Unlawful Associations
him from entering into a conspiracy with other people to destroy my home or to destroy society as a whole. Hon. members have referred to the position of organized labour and the churches, they have mentioned the petitions sent in here against section 98 of the criminal code, but they know perfectly well that there is nothing within the four corners of that section which would affect in the least degree any man who is willing to abide by the law and live as a decent Canadian should live. There is nothing against a man who is willing to endeavour to create harmony instead of distrust and disrespect.
For these reasons I shall vote to have section 98 of the criminal code left just as it is.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that those who advocate force when in power would have no hesitation in using it when out of power in order to gain their end if they had the opportunity, and so I am beginning to feel rather afraid of removing section 98 from the statute book. In anticipation of the success of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation at the next election, I would not be a bit surprised if we might not want to use section 98 against the unlawful assemblies of hon, gentlemen opposite who are now advocating the use of force against helpless people who have speeches to make. It is quite possible that this section will be of some use sooner or later.
The hon. member who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Nicholson) has indicated that a man is at liberty to use force in defence of his family and home. If the western farmer hears that it may create a great deal of trouble.
It certainly will when the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation tries to operate.

The western farmers may want to defend their homes against foreclosures, and they may quote the words of my hon. friend which gives them the liberty to use force in defence of their homes against foreclosures by sheriffs, and such like. He had better be careful or he may be getting into trouble.

ment of local inspectors would seem to be the best and cheapest way to carry on this work. The campaign which has been in progress for three years was carried out by officers stationed at Assiniboia, Indian Head, Saskatoon, Drum-heller -and Lethbridge.
